definition: Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a graph-based algorithm for efficient approximate nearest-neighbor search in high-dimensional vector spaces.
details: HNSW is one of the most widely used indexing algorithms in vector databases, offering a strong balance of search speed, accuracy, and memory usage.

explainer.lead: HNSW is a graph-based index for approximate nearest-neighbor search in high-dimensional vector spaces. It matters because it balances search speed, accuracy, and memory well enough to be one of the most widely used indexing algorithms in vector databases.

tiers.eli5: Think of shortcuts between towns on a map: start on a sparse network of long highways, then drop into denser local roads to reach the exact spot. HNSW does the same with vectors, hopping across a layered graph to get close fast, then refining.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers build the index over embeddings so a query touches only a small part of the graph instead of comparing against every vector. A common pitfall is that tuning for speed or memory trades away recall, so results are approximate rather than exact.
tiers.paperLevel: Vectors are nodes in a multi-layer graph; a search enters at the top layer and greedily descends to denser layers, keeping a bounded candidate list. It returns approximate neighbors, so there is no guarantee of finding the true nearest ones.

explainer.example: A vector database indexes a million document embeddings with HNSW; a query vector descends the layers, examines a small candidate set, and returns the closest matches in milliseconds.

citation.title: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs
citation.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
